# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

The first half of this comment is a valuable re-analysis.

- **Attrition.** It documents an attrition problem that, if the microdata are right, means the working paper misdescribed its own withdrawals.
- **Output measure.** It compares manager-reported output with organisations' own records and shows a systematic upward bias. In 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index was higher, which is very unlikely by chance (sign test, two-sided p ≈ 0.003).
- **Hours.** It replaces scheduled hours with logged hours and deflates the revenue comparison.

The sectoral argument (§5) is also correct. These are largely the problems I raised with the Halden paper, now backed by data.

The second half overreaches. The conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" is not supported by the comment's own corrected estimate. It is contradicted by the randomised evidence the comment cites selectively. It also misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are right:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% |
| Hours fall (27 organisations) | 34.6 / 40.3 | −14.1% |
| Hours fall (17 organisations) | 34.8 / 40.4 | −13.9% |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% |

There are three errors:

1. **The hours breakdown in §3 does not add up.**
   - Four scheduled 8-hour days plus 0.7 hours a day plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = 36.4 hours. The reported figure is 34.6.
   - Measured from baseline days (40.3 / 5 ≈ 8.06 hours) the total is even higher, at about 36.6.
   - Reaching 34.6 with 1.6 hours on the day off requires only about +0.25 hours a day on the other four days.
   - Either the per-day figure or the weekly total is wrong. This matters because it bears on the hours correction.
2. **The novelty extrapolation is off.** Energy falls from 0.61 SD to 0.29 SD in three months, about 0.107 SD a month. At that rate it reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten".
3. **The exit reasons are incomplete.** Six cited workload and two cited scheduling, which accounts for 8 of 9 withdrawals.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own results

After every correction the comment can actually make, a **10.8% gain in output per actual hour remains**. The comment attributes this to novelty but does not test that (see point 4). A residual it cannot explain away cannot support the claim that the gains are "entirely" an artifact. Adding "in our assessment" does not change this.

The bigger problem is the Varden trial. It addresses three of the comment's four explanations directly:

- **Selection:** offices were randomised; they did not volunteer.
- **Measurement:** output came from administrative records.
- **Hours:** actual hours came from timesheets.

Under all three, Varden found output per actual hour **rose 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4)** in case-processing offices at nine months. That is close to the comment's corrected 10.8%.

Even the counter stratum, which the comment calls "the most reliable finding in the literature", showed output per actual hour **rising 6.7% (CI +0.4 to +13.3)**. The comment quotes that stratum's fall in output per employee and leaves out its per-hour result. Varden's case-processing stratum is also more precise, with 14 offices to the counter stratum's 10. There is no basis for treating one stratum as the reliable finding and ignoring the other.

A conclusion consistent with the evidence would be roughly this: corrected per-hour gains are about half those reported, durability is unproven, and per-employee output falls in coverage-bound work.

## 2. The abstract claims a correction that was never made

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems lowers the gain to 10.8%. The first three are attrition, the output measure and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. No attrition correction appears anywhere, so the abstract overstates what was done.

The attrition finding deserves a quantitative treatment. With 70 enrolled organisations, an intention-to-treat bound is feasible. For example, assume the nine withdrawals had output at the retail level, or at 80, and show the effect on the overall estimate. That would turn a strong qualitative point into a number.

## 3. Table 2 mixes sample changes with corrections

Each row of Table 2 uses a different set of organisations: 61, 23, 27 and 17. The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore combines two things:

- the effect of the corrections;
- differences between the subsets.

The Data Note says the subsets are not random, but the abstract and conclusion compare across them anyway. The clean decomposition uses the 17 organisations with both records and time tracking:

| Row | Output | Hours |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Manager-reported | Scheduled |
| 2 | Record-based | Scheduled |
| 3 | Manager-reported | Actual |
| 4 | Record-based | Actual |

The comment should also report how those 17 compare with the rest on sector, size and manager-reported output. The 27 with time tracking had a manager-reported index of 98.4, slightly below the pilot average of 98.7, so they may not be unusually favourable.

## 4. The novelty argument is asserted, not tested

- **Energy is not output.** The decline in self-reported energy is suggestive, but the claim is about productivity. The Halden output index was collected **monthly**, so the microdata can show whether output per hour declined from month 1 to month 6. That is the direct test, and the comment does not report it.
- **Two points do not establish a trend.** A straight line through months 3 and 6 assumes the decline continues at the same rate. A decline that levels off above zero fits equally well.
- **Varden's timing weighs against it, weakly.** Varden's case-processing gain was measured at month nine. That is beyond the point where this extrapolation puts energy back at baseline, in a setting where staff did not choose the change. It is a different population, but it is the only evidence available past six months.
- **The burden of proof applies both ways.** The comment is right that six months cannot show the effect is durable. But that only means the question is open. Asserting that the effect is entirely due to novelty is itself a positive claim that needs evidence.

## 5. §7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis

| The comment says | The Varden paper says |
|---|---|
| The analysis was "selected for analysis after the results were known" | Calendar data were collected **in month six at managers' request**, before the nine-month results |
| The meetings finding is being "cited as a mechanism" | The authors said it "cannot establish a mechanism", labelled it unregistered, stressed it rests on seven offices, and registered a confirmatory test for 24 months |

The comment's underlying caution is fair. With 7 offices, r = 0.71 has a 95% interval of roughly −0.09 to 0.95. But the Varden authors already made that caveat themselves. The comment should criticise the analysis as it was presented. It might also note that in the Halden interviews, 47 of 58 managers independently mentioned meeting cuts, which is weak but separate support.

The meetings hypothesis also cuts against the comment's argument. If the gain comes from removing low-value meetings, it is a real gain in output per paid hour from changing how work is organised. That is neither a measurement artifact nor novelty.

## 6. Organisations' records are better than manager ratings, but not ground truth

The 3.8-point gap is persuasive evidence of bias in the manager ratings. But treating the record-based index as true output has two problems:

- **Some records measure inputs.** "Billable hours delivered" is closer to a measure of time worked than of output. In a trial that cuts hours, it biases output downward. Results should be shown with and without organisations whose records measure hours.
- **Records are narrower than what managers rate.** Counts of tickets or cases can miss outputs that managers' overall judgement includes. The gap shows managers rated higher than the records, not necessarily that managers overstated true output.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Retail.** The 11.2% fall rests on 3 organisations. Comparing it with Varden's −11.4% also mixes measures: Halden's is an unadjusted output index for each organisation, Varden's is output per FTE relative to a control group. The closeness of the two numbers is coincidental and shouldn't be presented as replication.
- **Revenue deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue; sector producer prices would be better. The direction of the correction is right regardless.
- **Unlogged work on days off.** The note that some day-off work is probably unrecorded is fair. It implies the true per-hour gain is somewhat below 10.8%, and saying so would strengthen the comment's position honestly.

## Suggested revision of the conclusion

> Using the pilot microdata, we find that the working paper misdescribed attrition, that manager-reported output exceeded record-based output in 19 of 23 organisations, and that actual hours fell by about 14% rather than 20%. In the 17 organisations where both corrections are possible, the implied gain in output per actual hour is about 11%, less than half the reported figure. Whether this residual persists beyond six months is untested; the declining energy measure is consistent with a novelty effect, and the pilot's monthly output data should be used to test for one directly. The randomised Varden trial finds per-hour gains of similar size under record-based output and actual hours, alongside clear losses of output per employee in coverage-bound work. The evidence supports substantially smaller per-hour gains than pilots have reported, not their absence.

The recommendations in §8 are sound as they stand. Analysing all enrolled organisations, including those that withdrew, is especially important given the attrition finding.
